prompt: Roda Livre’s database is slow at six in the evening, and Davi moves it to one machine with twice the cores and memory. What has he done?
hint: One machine before, one machine after.

choices.text: Scaled out, because the capacity went up without the software changing
choices.why: Out means more machines, and then the software has to know there are several.

choices.text: Scaled up, keeping the software exactly as it was, on a larger computer
choices.why: Right: a bigger machine, and nothing in the software had to change.

choices.text: Partitioned the database, since the data now has more room
choices.why: Partitioning splits data over several machines; there is still one.

choices.text: Replicated it, because the old machine still holds a copy
choices.why: Nothing keeps the old machine in step; a replica receives every change.

prompt: Which of these problems arrives with a second machine, and did not exist with one?
hint: Think about what travels between them.

choices.text: A disk that fills up with data
choices.why: One machine’s disk fills up just as well.

choices.text: A slow query over a large table
choices.why: A single machine has slow queries of its own.

choices.text: A request whose reply never comes, leaving the sender unsure whether it was done
choices.why: Right: a function call returns or raises; a message over a network just goes quiet.

choices.text: A program with a bug in it
choices.why: Bugs need no network.

prompt: The dock sensor stamps a docking at 08:00:00.400, and the app’s server stamps the next unlock of the same bicycle at 08:00:00.100. What explains it?
hint: Two stamps, two machines.

choices.text: The bicycle was unlocked before it was docked, and the data is right
choices.why: A bicycle has to arrive at a dock before it leaves it.

choices.text: The sensor’s clock and the server’s clock disagree
choices.why: Right: the sensor runs ahead of the server, and the order in the data is wrong.

choices.text: The network lost the docking message, and the sensor sent it again later
choices.why: A resent message keeps the time the sensor stamped on it.

choices.text: The sensor rounds its times to the nearest second
choices.why: Both stamps carry milliseconds.

prompt: Roda Livre’s data fits on a laptop. Why does its data team still need to understand distributed systems?
hint: Think about what the team rents.

choices.text: Because it will need a cluster within a year, as the number of bicycles grows
choices.why: Davi’s rule is one machine until it hurts, and nothing says it will hurt.

choices.text: Because a laptop is not allowed to hold customer data
choices.why: Where the data is kept is a question of security, not of distribution.

choices.text: The services it rents, like the warehouse, are distributed underneath
choices.why: Right: the warehouse, object storage and a message log all are.

choices.text: Because every data engineering job involves running a cluster by hand
choices.why: Most teams rent the cluster and never touch a machine of it.

prompt: What decides which partition a row goes to?
hint: It is a column.

choices.text: The order in which rows arrived, so that each partition fills in turn
choices.why: That is the cake picture: every question would then ask every partition.

choices.text: The size of the row in bytes, so that partitions stay the same size
choices.why: Size says nothing about which questions the row answers.

choices.text: The machine with the most free disk at the moment of the write
choices.why: Then nobody could find the row again without asking every machine.

choices.text: The value of its partition key
choices.why: Right: by its range, or by its hash.

prompt: Rides are partitioned by date, one partition per day. At six on a busy Friday evening, which partition receives the writes?
hint: Every new ride has today’s date.

choices.text: All of them evenly, because a partition key spreads the writes
choices.why: A range key keeps neighbours together, and today’s rides are neighbours.

choices.text: Today’s alone, since every ride starting now carries today’s date
choices.why: Right: that is the weakness of range partitioning on a date.

choices.text: The one with the fewest rows, since the database balances new writes
choices.why: The key decides, not the current size.

choices.text: Yesterday’s, until midnight creates today’s
choices.why: A ride on Friday has Friday’s date.

prompt: Rides are hash-partitioned by ride id over four machines. Marta asks for every ride of the second week of September. How many partitions are read?
hint: Where did the hash put that week’s rides?

choices.text: One, the partition that holds that week
choices.why: That is range partitioning by date; a hash scatters the week.

choices.text: Two, because a week spans two hash values
choices.why: Each ride id gets its own hash; the week is all over the place.

choices.text: All four: a hash scatters that week’s rides everywhere
choices.why: Right: neighbouring keys are scattered, so a range question asks everybody.

choices.text: None, because an index on one machine answers it
choices.why: The rides themselves are on four machines.

prompt: Match each term to what it means.
hint: Two are about how; two are about what.

pairs.right: the column whose value picks the partition
a database’s word for a partition

prompt: In the capture of `skew.py`, how many rides did ST02 have?
hint: The last line of the output.

prompt: Partitioned by hash of the station, partition 3 held 4730 rides. Why did hashing not even it out?
hint: Look at what is being hashed.

choices.text: MD5 is a weak hash function and sends too many keys to partition 3
choices.why: Partition 3 got three stations; the trouble is that one of them is ST02.

choices.text: Every ST02 ride carries the same key, so all of them share one partition
choices.why: Right: the same key goes to the same partition, every time.

choices.text: Four partitions are too few; with eight, ST02’s rides would have been split
choices.why: With eight, ST02 would still go to exactly one of them.

choices.text: That line of the program used range partitioning by mistake
choices.why: It calls `by_hash`; the range row is the one above it.

prompt: Switching the partition key to the ride id evened the partitions out. What did it cost?
hint: Ask a question about one station.

choices.text: Nothing, since ride ids are unique and every question got cheaper
choices.why: A question per station got dearer: it now reads four partitions.

choices.text: A question about one station now asks all four partitions
choices.why: Right: the even load moved the cost to the station question.

choices.text: The rides of a station are lost when one partition fails
choices.why: Losing a partition is replication’s subject, and loses data whatever the key.

choices.text: Ride ids take longer to hash than station ids
choices.why: Both are short strings; the difference is not where the cost went.

prompt: Twelve stations hashed into four partitions left partition 0 with a single station. What does that show?
hint: Count the keys.

choices.text: ST10 is a hot station
choices.why: Partition 0 held 544 rides, the fewest of the four.

choices.text: The hash function misbehaves on keys that start with the same letters
choices.why: MD5 scatters similar keys well; ride ids start alike too and came out even.

choices.text: Hash partitioning needs a number as its key, not text
choices.why: The program hashes text, and it works for ride ids.

choices.text: Twelve keys are too few to share out evenly
choices.why: Right: a hash is even over thousands of keys, not over twelve.

prompt: Splitting a hot key into `ST02#0` to `ST02#3`, so that its rows land on several partitions, is called ___.
hint: A word from cooking.

prompt: By modulo, how many of the 10,000 rides changed node when the fifth node joined?
hint: The `modulo` line of the capture.

prompt: With `hash % N`, why do about four keys in five move when N goes from 4 to 5?
hint: Compare two remainders.

choices.text: The new node copies four fifths of the data so that it starts balanced
choices.why: It ends up with a fifth; the rest moved between old nodes.

choices.text: It stays only where the remainder after dividing by 4 equals the one after dividing by 5
choices.why: Right: that happens for four numbers in twenty.

choices.text: The hash of every key changes when the number of nodes changes
choices.why: The hash depends on the key alone; the remainder is what changes.

choices.text: The old nodes delete their data and load it again from the start
choices.why: Keys whose remainder agrees stay put.

prompt: On the ring, a new node lands between two others. Which node do the keys it takes come from?
hint: Before it joined, where did those keys walk to?

choices.text: A fifth from each of the old nodes, so that all stay equal
choices.why: Only the arc in front of the new node changes hands.

choices.text: The node before it on the ring
choices.why: Keys belong to the first node clockwise after them, and that was never the one before.

choices.text: The next node clockwise
choices.why: Right: those keys used to walk on to it, and now meet the new node first.

choices.text: Whichever node holds the most keys at the moment it joins
choices.why: Placement follows the hash of the node’s name, not the loads.

prompt: With one point per node, the arcs of a ring come out uneven. What is done about it?
hint: `ring(nodes, points=100)`.

choices.text: Nodes are added until the arcs even out by chance
choices.why: More nodes means more arcs, still one per node and still uneven.

choices.text: Keys are moved by hand from the busiest node each night
choices.why: Then a key’s place would no longer follow from its hash.

choices.text: Each node is put on the ring at many points instead of one
choices.why: Right: virtual nodes, whose many small arcs add up close to a fair share.

choices.text: The system goes back to hash modulo N, which is even
choices.why: It is even, and it moves four keys in five on every change.

prompt: Which of these does the ring’s line of the capture show? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the `ring` lines.

choices.text: 2177 rides moved
choices.why: Yes, all of them to `n5`.

choices.text: No ride moved between old nodes
choices.why: Yes: `0 between old ones`.

choices.text: Each node ended with exactly 2000 rides
choices.why: They ended between 1622 and 2177.

choices.text: More rides moved than with modulo
choices.why: Modulo moved 7966.

prompt: Somebody runs a `DELETE` on the rides table by mistake. What do the followers do?
hint: They replay the leader’s log.

choices.text: Keep the rows, since a replica is a backup of the data from before
choices.why: That is the wrong picture: a backup is a copy from before, kept apart.

choices.text: Refuse the change, because followers accept writes only from the app
choices.why: Followers take every change from the leader’s log.

choices.text: Delete the same rows
choices.why: Right: a mistake replicates as faithfully as a correct write.

choices.text: Hold the change until a person approves it
choices.why: Nothing in replication waits for a person.

prompt: The leader confirms each write at once and the followers catch up afterwards. What goes wrong when the leader dies?
hint: What had it not sent yet?

choices.text: Every write had been waiting for the slowest follower
choices.why: That is the cost of synchronous replication, and this is the other kind.

choices.text: The writes it confirmed but had not sent are lost
choices.why: Right: confirmed to the client, never sent to a follower.

choices.text: The followers stop accepting reads until it comes back
choices.why: Followers go on answering reads, and one of them is promoted.

choices.text: Reads sent to it had been returning old values
choices.why: The leader is the one copy that is never behind.

prompt: In `replica.py`, how many milliseconds behind the leader does the follower run?
hint: The first line after the file name.

prompt: ana docks her bicycle, and the app tells her the ride is still running. Which remedy fits?
hint: She is the one person who knows the answer.

choices.text: Add more followers, so that one of them is current when she reads
choices.why: Every follower replays the same log, late.

choices.text: Send her reads to a different follower each time she asks
choices.why: Each one may be behind, and by different amounts.

choices.text: Read her own recent changes from the leader, not a follower
choices.why: Right: read-your-writes, for a while after she writes.

choices.text: Give her reads a shorter timeout
choices.why: The follower answered at once, with the old value.

prompt: A leader is cut off from the others but keeps running, and a follower is promoted in its place. What is the danger?
hint: How many machines think they are the leader?

choices.text: The promoted follower refuses reads until the old leader returns
choices.why: A promoted follower serves reads and writes at once.

choices.text: The new leader erases the old leader’s data when it is promoted
choices.why: Neither machine can reach the other to erase anything.

choices.text: Two leaders accept writes for the same data at once
choices.why: Right: split brain, for as long as the old one believes it leads.

choices.text: None, since a promoted follower always has every write
choices.why: With asynchronous replication it is missing the last ones.

prompt: With N = 3, which pair guarantees that a read sees the last write?
hint: R + W > N.

choices.why: R + W = 3, which is not greater than 3: two reads in three.
R + W = 3 again: one read in three misses.
Right: 4 is greater than 3, so every read set overlaps the write set.
The first line of the capture: one read in three.

prompt: With W = 1 and R = 1, how many of the three possible reads saw ST06 in the capture?
hint: The first line.

prompt: N = 3, W = 3, R = 1. One replica goes down. What still works?
hint: Count what each side needs.

choices.text: Writes, because one replica is enough to confirm them
choices.why: W = 3: a write needs every replica, and one is down.

choices.text: Reads and writes, as two replicas are still a majority of three
choices.why: A majority is enough only when W asks for a majority.

choices.text: Reads, since a read needs one replica and two are still up
choices.why: Right: a read needs one replica; a write needs all three.

choices.text: Neither
choices.why: Two replicas are still up, and a read asks one.

prompt: A read is certain to meet the last write when R + W is greater than ___.
hint: How many replicas hold each piece of data?

prompt: With a one-second timeout, the slow node and the hung node printed the same line. What does that show?
hint: One of them would have answered.

choices.text: Both nodes had crashed before the probe reached them
choices.why: The slow one answered at five seconds.

choices.text: The slow node was hung too, since it answered nothing
choices.why: It answered once the client waited long enough.

choices.text: Waiting cannot tell a node that is late from one that will never answer
choices.why: Right: it says how long you waited, not what happened.

choices.text: `probe.py` has a bug that hides the real error
choices.why: The real error is the silence; there is nothing else to show.

prompt: Port 8003 answered `Connection refused` at once. Why is that more informative than a timeout?
hint: Somebody had to send it.

choices.text: It proves the whole machine is switched off
choices.why: A switched-off machine sends nothing back at all.

choices.text: It is a reply, so a running machine sent it back
choices.why: Right: the machine is up and nothing listens on that port.

choices.text: It means the network between the two machines is cut
choices.why: Across a cut link no reply arrives, and that is a timeout.

choices.text: It shows the node is slow and will answer later
choices.why: The slow node was on port 8001, and it timed out like the hung one.

prompt: Match each situation on the far side to what it is.
hint: Only one of them sends anything back.

pairs.left: the process or the machine has stopped
both machines fine, the link between them cut
alive and working, three seconds late
a running machine with nothing on the port

prompt: A team sets its heartbeat timeout very short, to fail over faster. What happens on a busy day?
hint: Busy nodes answer late.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since a shorter timeout only finds dead nodes sooner
choices.why: It also declares slow nodes dead, and busy days make nodes slow.

choices.text: Healthy leaders that are only slow get replaced
choices.why: Right: and each failover adds work to machines already busy.

choices.text: Failovers stop, because heartbeats are then sent less often
choices.why: The timeout is how long to wait, not how often to send.

choices.text: Clients see fewer errors, as dead nodes are found sooner
choices.why: They see more: every needless failover interrupts them.

prompt: Which of these is idempotent?
hint: Do it twice and compare.

choices.text: Adding a fare to a customer’s bill
choices.why: Twice is two fares.

choices.text: Setting dock 4 at Batel to empty, whatever it was before
choices.why: Right: set it twice and it is still empty.

choices.text: Appending a ride to the end of a log file
choices.why: Twice is the ride in the log twice.

choices.text: Adding one to a station’s count of rides
choices.why: Twice adds two.

prompt: Without a request id, how many cents did the ledger hold for one ride?
hint: Three charges of 450.

prompt: Why does the client in `retry.py` send the same request id on every attempt?
hint: What would a new id look like to the ledger?

choices.text: So that the server answers faster, having seen the id before
choices.why: The id changes what is recorded, not how fast.

choices.text: Because making a new id each time would be slower
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it; a new id would make a new charge.

choices.text: Because the database limits each ride to one request id
choices.why: The `UNIQUE` is on the request, not on the ride.

choices.text: So a retry is recognised as a repeat
choices.why: Right: one charge meant, one id, however many attempts.

prompt: Why add jitter to the backoff between retries?
hint: Picture a thousand clients failing at the same moment.

choices.text: So clients that failed together retry apart
choices.why: Right: otherwise they all come back in the same instant.

choices.text: To make each wait shorter than the one before it
choices.why: The backoff doubles; the jitter only scatters it.

choices.text: To hide from the server how many times a client has retried
choices.why: The server sees every attempt anyway.

choices.text: To give each attempt a fresh request id
choices.why: A fresh id on a retry is the mistake the section warns about.

prompt: Put in order what happens when `retry.py` runs without a request id and the first reply is lost.
hint: The charge comes before the silence.
items: the client waits and sends again
trap: The charge is recorded before the reply is lost, which is why the retry charges twice.

prompt: An operation whose second run changes nothing is called ___.
hint: The property that makes a retry safe.

prompt: With plan B, how many records crossed the network?
hint: Thirty-six partial counts, twelve already home.

prompt: Which of these can each node compute on its own rides first, for the results to be combined afterwards?
hint: Will the pieces add up?

choices.text: The median ride length per station
choices.why: The median of three medians is not the median of all the rides.

choices.text: The total cents charged per station
choices.why: Right: a sum adds up in pieces, like a count.

choices.text: The number of different customers who rode from each station
choices.why: A customer seen on two nodes would be counted twice when the pieces are added.

choices.text: The ride length below which 90% of rides fall, per station
choices.why: Like a median, it needs the values together, not partial results.

choices.text: Plan A compresses one ride in three before sending

prompt: A leaderless store picks the newest version by the time of the write, taken from each client’s clock. What is the risk?
hint: Two clients, two clocks.

choices.text: Reads become slower, because comparing times costs more than comparing counters
choices.why: The comparison is cheap either way; what it compares is the trouble.

choices.text: A client whose clock is behind writes a value that loses to an older one
choices.why: Right: the newer write carries the smaller time, and the read keeps the old value.

choices.text: Nothing changes, as long as R + W is greater than N
choices.why: The overlap finds every version; the clock then picks the wrong one.

choices.text: Writes need more replicas to confirm them
